title: Aligning Language Model Benchmarks with Pairwise Preferences
claim: A misaligned benchmark ranking is fixed by learning item weights from source models' pairwise preferences, then applying them to unseen models.
layout: 3 sections, left-to-right: misaligned problem panel, BenchAlign pipeline, aligned result panel; arrows between stages
description: A wide, three-part figure read left to right. The left rounded box, titled 'Misaligned Benchmark', stacks a red-tinted 'Benchmark Ranking' (A > B > C) above a green 'Target Preference' (C > A > B), with a not-equal sign between them. The middle box shows source-model response grids (check marks and crosses) for models A, B and C, plus target pairwise preferences (C > A, A > B). A brace and arrow lead into a small neural network labeled BenchAlign. Its output is a green 'Predicted Item Relevance' bar. A multiplication sign combines that bar with a response grid for unobserved models D, E and F. A final arrow leads to the right panel, 'Aligned Benchmark', where the benchmark ranking (D > E > F) is green and equals the target preference. Model icons are small network glyphs. Red marks misalignment and green marks alignment.
caption: Overview of BenchAlign as a diagnostic tool for studying benchmark alignment. Given a benchmark whose ranking of target models is misaligned with a target preference, we use source models and their pairwise preferences to learn question weights via learning-to-rank. The reweighted benchmark is then evaluated to assess whether the induced ranking aligns with the target preference.
abstract: Language model benchmarks are pervasive and computationally-efficient proxies for real-world downstream performance. However, many recent works find that benchmarks often fail to predict downstream utility. While some works have begun diagnosing sources of misalignment, there remain no ways to systematically update benchmarks to align their scores with downstream usage. Towards bridging this gap, we introduce and study \textit{benchmark alignment}, where we use information about downstream model performance to automatically update benchmarks, specifically aiming to update static benchmarks so they generalizably rank models according to new pairwise preferences. Our experiments involving 4576 language models and 6 benchmarks show that reweighting benchmark items can successfully rank unseen models, even generalizing across model scales in most cases. And while naive alignment unsurprisingly requires large numbers of models and benchmark questions, an oracle experiment suggests this could be reduced to as few as 20 well-chosen models. Overall, our work takes a step towards efficiently aligning benchmark development with downstream tasks. All of our code, models, and data are publicly-available: https://github.com/hartvigsen-group/benchalign
